speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These include a measure announced in the 2018 Budget, as well as five changes arising from periodic reviews of the GST regime to ease business compliance, clarify existing legislation and improve tax administration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We sought views from the public on the draft Bill earlier this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, GST is applicable on services only in instances where the service is supplied in Singapore, essentially when the supplier has an establishment in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With the digital economy, it has become increasingly common for services to be supplied by overseas suppliers, without the need for the suppliers to establish a presence within Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We welcome this development, as it allows businesses and consumers to have access to services from overseas suppliers readily.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But at the same time, we must ensure that our tax rules are updated, such that both imported and local services are treated on a level playing field and accorded the same GST treatment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To ensure smooth implementation of the measures, MOF and the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) have consulted extensively with businesses as well as industry associations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I will explain in greater detail how these measures work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Normally, GST-registered businesses will charge and collect GST on their supplies of services to customers, and then they will pay the GST collected to IRAS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But GST is not charged by overseas suppliers as they are not registered for GST in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we have proposed a Reverse Charge mechanism where local business customers that are GST-registered and purchase services from overseas suppliers will instead be responsible for accounting and paying the GST to IRAS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why it is called Reverse Charge because instead of having the supplier account for and pay the GST as it is traditionally done, we are now asking the customer to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Examples of B2B imported services include management, information technology (IT) and payroll services charged by overseas service providers to local business customers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I should clarify that the vast majority of local businesses purchasing services from overseas suppliers will not be affected by Reverse Charge.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is because we will not apply Reverse Charge on businesses which can claim full refund of the GST they incur on their purchases, including imported services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, such businesses need not pay the GST on imported services, only then to claim a full GST refund later.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Essentially, they are paying and then claiming in full, so really, there is no need to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And that is why we are not applying reverse charge on such businesses, and this will avoid unnecessary compliance burden for these businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Instead, businesses affected by Reverse Charge are primarily those that are not entitled to full GST refund in the first place, for instance, when they make GST-exempt supplies, and these affected businesses are mainly financial institutions and residential property developers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, earlier, the Reverse Charge was for B2B.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These GST-registered overseas vendors will then charge and collect GST on their sale of digital services to consumers in Singapore and pay the GST they collect to IRAS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Examples of such B2C imported digital services are video and music streaming services, mobile applications and software.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Reverse Charge and OVR are not new and have already been adopted in several jurisdictions with Value-Added Tax (VAT) or GST regimes, such as Australia, New Zealand, Japan and Korea.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These measures are also consistent with international guidelines for consumption taxes to address the tax challenges of the global economy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For B2C services provided to consumers, the scope is targeted and, as mentioned earlier, covers only digital services like video and music streaming services, mobile applications and software.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Such digital services form a small share of current consumption expenditure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As mentioned earlier, MOF also regularly reviews and refines the GST regime, and the Bill provides for other changes to existing tax policies and administration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, similar to the amendments introduced in the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill 2018, which were passed in Parliament last month, we will enhance IRAS’ powers to investigate tax crimes for GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Tax offenders and criminal syndicates are employing more sophisticated schemes to defraud the authorities, as I mentioned in my last speech when I passed the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And so, enhanced investigative powers are required to more effectively deal with serious tax offenders, as well as acts of obstruction which may hamper IRAS' investigations and prosecution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Similar to the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill 2018, we will put in place safeguards in the way these enhanced legislative powers are exercised.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: All these enhanced investigative powers may only be exercised by officers authorised by the Comptroller of GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These authorised officers will receive training consistent with those in other law enforcement agencies, like Singapore Customs and Singapore Police Force.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The amendments will also expand IRAS' power to gather from any person all information relevant to its investigations or the prosecution of offences under the GST Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, for GST purposes, IRAS may gather information relating to a person’s business transactions only.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The amendment will allow IRAS to gather all information as long as it is relevant to the investigation or prosecution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, this could include information relating to a person’s income or assets, or information relating to accomplices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 3, 33 and 34 of the Bill provide for all of the changes to enhance IRAS' powers to investigate tax crimes which I have just described.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The second broad change pertains to the proposed amendment of the GST Act to allow IRAS to share with law enforcement agencies (LEAs) information that may be relevant to the investigation or prosecution of serious crimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Such crimes are prescribed in the First and Second Schedules to the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Likewise, this proposal was introduced in the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill 2018.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Again, other countries, like Australia, Norway, Sweden and the UK, also allow for the disclosure of tax information to LEAs to combat non-tax crimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The information shared is to be disclosed by the Comptroller to the head of an LEA for the purpose of the investigation or prosecution of serious crimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Unauthorised onward disclosure of such information constitutes an offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clause 4 of the Bill provides for the changes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Lastly, we propose to amend the GST Act to strengthen prosecution and deterrence of unauthorised collection of GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, an offence is committed if a non-GST registered person issues an invoice or receipt with an amount purporting to be GST.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Such an offence is currently punishable by a penalty and a fine.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This, in turn, allows the use of alternative evidence, such as sales contracts or service agreements, in proving unauthorised GST collection.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The custodial sentence of not exceeding three years is aligned with existing penalties under the GST Act, which are similarly committed through negligence or without reasonable excuse.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This ensures that GST-registered businesses exercise due responsibility when charging and collecting GST on their supplies made and also deters the abuse of a company’s GST-registration status.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 30 to 32 of the Bill provides for this change.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In general, I am supportive of the amendments, which largely are to impose GST on imported services, and to facilitate and enhance the powers of IRAS to combat tax evasion and crimes.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are very much welcome, particularly with the rise in the purchase and consumption of products and services through digital means and e-commerce platforms, and the higher potential for tax evasion and cyber-related tax crimes.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nonetheless, I seek some clarifications from the Ministry and I have one suggestion to offer for consideration for future amendments to the GST Act.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will help in creating parity between imported and local products and services.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, may I seek the Ministry's clarification on a few things?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, are all of our current locally provided services and products through digital means or e-commerce platforms, whether B2B or B2C, done by GST-registered entities?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Two, what is the number of individuals selling products or services locally through digital means or e-commerce platforms who are not running GST-registered entities?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Three, what is the number of local entities selling products or services locally or overseas through digital means or e-commerce platforms which are not GST-registered, but which are charging local GST on their customers?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Four, are these areas of concern for the Ministry, and, if so, how does the Ministry intend to address them?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the Ministry address GST collection, even without evidence of invoices given to the customer, such as through online payments or transfers?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are the above examples of business transactions resulting in any loss of GST revenue?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry consider imposing higher GST rates for such luxury items, where the price tiers and corresponding GST rates can be decided through engaging Singaporeans in focus group discussions and eliciting their views?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Besides, we have already imposed differential tax rates for housing, for instance, where residences that cost less than $1 million are charged a 3% Buyer's Stamp Duty, while those that cost more than $1 million are charged a 4% Buyer's Stamp Duty.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, it has been done for housing, and can we now extend such differential GST or tax rates to other luxury items, too, such as cars, for instance?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, there are other items, such as alcoholic beverages and tobacco products, which can have an impact on social behaviour and which can be imposed with differential GST rates.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To elaborate, tobacco products, such as packed cigarettes, can be imposed with a GST rate of 10% at the minimum, while cigars, which are usually consumed by the more affluent, can have a higher GST rate of 12%-15%, for instance.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Likewise, alcoholic beverages can be imposed with a GST rate of 10% at the minimum and gradually increased depending on the alcohol content of the beverage.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Again, the price tiers and corresponding GST rates for these tobacco products and alcoholic beverages can be decided through engaging Singaporeans in focus group discussions and eliciting their views and suggestions.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Tobacco products and alcoholic beverages are not daily necessities, and in order to nurture a healthier lifestyle and a more positive social behaviour, differential GST rates can be imposed so as to encourage individuals to choose alcoholic beverages of lower alcohol content, for instance, and eventually give up smoking because it would simply be too expensive a habit to have.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Over the recent years, Singapore's e-commerce industry has been growing steadily.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: GST is an important source of revenue for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The proposed extended coverage to ensure that GST is collected for services purchased overseas serves to ensure that our GST system remains fair and resilient in this digital economy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unlike advertising on traditional media platforms, online advertising services offer advertisers the ability to target individuals with specifically tailored messages.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even if the advertiser intended for the advertisements to be substantially promulgated here, it might be hard to prove this if the authorities are only able to see a small subset of the advertisements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Programmatic advertising is another key trend in the industry, whereby software is used to buy digital advertisements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For such advertisements, the one making the decision to show the advertisement to the individuals is an algorithm, rather than a person.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How would the authority calculate the GST payable if an online marketplace sells a mix of services that both incur and are exempt from GST?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If it is based on self-declaration, how would the authorities ensure against under-declaration?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to ask if consultancy or advisory services offered through such online marketplaces would attract GST.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With e-commerce posing as a serious disruption to traditional retailers, perhaps the Ministry could consider ensuring a level playing field for local merchants who are required to incorporate GST, as compared to their online competitors who do not need to.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, it raises a number of important questions.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Digital services are becoming an increasingly central part of our lives.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We all use mobile apps multiple times a day.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: From games to health tracking, to stock market information services, we hardly even notice them anymore.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When you add up all the value of all the digital services, including software, entertainment, online learning and search engines, the total value is mind-boggling.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At one level, the imposition of GST on overseas providers is a simple matter of levelling the playing field.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is because they have to charge GST while their overseas counterparts do not have to.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They may decide to abandon local providers for foreign ones in pursuit of what they think to be a 7% "discount".

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For businesses, most businesses can claim back GST.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, many small businesses may not be registered and, hence, behave essentially like consumers.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, the idea, while bold, is fundamentally sound.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But the relatively novel nature raises a number of critical questions.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: First, how do we ensure even and effective implementation of this regime?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The implication is that many small companies will be liable under our regime.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In particular, I am concerned about small marketplaces.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Their actual revenues may only be a small fraction of the turnover on their site.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Will the Ministry review this threshold and adjust it if it is found to create problems?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And, if not, will there be a mechanism to review it periodically, and adjust it when expedient?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The next question has to do with efficiency of the new tax.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We all know that spending on digital services is growing rapidly.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But how much of that would fall under this regime and how much taxes would be generated for our national coffers?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: More importantly, what is the cost of monitoring and enforcing compliance?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Do IRAS and the other relevant authorities have the capabilities and the capacity?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Digital service startups are proliferating, with thousands appearing every day.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There could be potentially millions of small GST payers all around the globe.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How will we inform all the affected companies and marketplaces about their liabilities under our GST regime?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How will we monitor that all relevant vendors are complying with this regime?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And how will we enforce penalties for non-compliance, given that they have no presence in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Is there a risk that service providers may thumb their noses at Singapore and they basically say to IRAS "catch me if you can"?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A global tax regime of this nature is likely to be complex.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Will the revenue raised justify the expenditure on monitoring, collecting and enforcing the tax?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A related question is on providers abandoning Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Would active enforcement result in some companies simply deciding not to serve Singapore-based consumers?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Small and innovative overseas startups may not be willing to invest in the costs of compliance.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They may simply decide not to serve a small market like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This could potentially deprive local companies and consumers of cutting-edge technology.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Under the new rules, Overseas Vendors are required to obtain and maintain at least two pieces of non-conflicting evidence of customers' location: Payment Proxy, Residence Proxy and Access Proxy.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is easy to imagine smaller companies saying, "forget it, Singapore customers are just not worth this trouble".

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in the European Union (EU) was seen as onerous.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There were stories of businesses that simply turned away EU customers when GDPR was introduced.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They felt that compliance was just too cumbersome.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And that was for a market of 500 million people!

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One possible consequence is that Singapore-based customers may resort to evasion tactics.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They could use Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), online credit cards and overseas post office (P O) boxes in order to be able to access these services.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This opens them to the risk of penalties.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The regime states that non-GST registered customers should not provide incorrect or false information to the Overseas Vendors.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: According to IRAS, "customer misrepresentation is a serious offence, and offenders may face heavy penalties".

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What penalties are envisaged, and how will they be enforced?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Unlike people bringing in undeclared goods, there will not be any physical evidence to rely on.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The final question is a familiar one on the impact of such a tax on some consumers.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we are optimists, we could argue that this broadens the tax base.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It makes our tax regime more progressive by generating revenue from overseas companies.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This would free up additional resources for beneficial programmes.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can reduce other taxes that disproportionately burden lower-income groups that are already under stress.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, there is a potential dark side to such a tax.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is increasing concern about a "digital divide".

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Lower-income groups are going to be disadvantaged because they lack exposure to the digital world.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some digital services may also act as more affordable substitutes for physical services.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, online learning and education and even online entertainment.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And such experiences are critical to survive and to thrive in the world of Industry 4.0.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As Singapore prepares itself for the new digital economy, I would like to applaud the Government for having the vision and the courage to undertake this bold initiative.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The issue of GST for online commerce is a major one, and the international debate in western countries has been going on for more than a decade.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Originally, exemption was given by many governments because of the difficulty of enforcement, as well as the desire to promote online commerce.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, online commerce has taken off in a way in many countries, including Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Now the pendulum has swung to the other side, which is that the major online commerce companies are threatening the survival of many brick-and-mortar businesses.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Online commerce is here to stay, and brick and mortar businesses have no choice but to adapt.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our SMEs, especially the micro-SMEs in our HDB heartland, are facing tremendous challenges these few years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Their existence, or not, will impact the fabric of our society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Having said all that, the SMEs I speak to know that they must adapt.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, on the design of GST for imported services and how the measures can be effective.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Both Mr Ong Teng Koon and Mr Melvin Yong raised questions on how such a regime – GST for imported services – can be effectively implemented.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, let me highlight a few salient aspects of the design of the proposed measure that will enable us to ensure effective implementation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, Singapore adopts, as Members are aware, a broad-based single rate GST regime with few exemptions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This provides a good foundation for businesses to comply with the new GST rules for imported services without much need to classify and ascertain the applicable GST treatment, as the same GST rate applies to most transactions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We build on this foundation by learning from the experience of other jurisdictions and consulting extensively with industry players on how rules may be formulated to impose minimal compliance burden.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These include the Business Industry Advisory Committee to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), the Singapore Retailers Association (SRA) and the Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS).

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, where possible, we have ensured consistency in our rules with those of other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This eases compliance, promotes effectiveness and provides certainty for the industry.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, the scope of digital services that is subject to GST as well as the definition of electronic marketplace operators under the OVR regime are generally aligned with that in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Third, our rules ensure that we do not impose unnecessary GST liability on businesses.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I mentioned just now, under reverse charge for B2B imported services, we do away with the need for local businesses to account for GST on the services they import if they can already claim a full refund of GST incurred on their purchases.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we put in place a two-tier registration threshold for the OVR regime for B2C imported services, which is based on global annual turnover and sales to Singapore customers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These features enable us to focus our enforcement of GST for imported services on these overseas vendors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is also in line with the concern highlighted by Mr Ong Teng Koon on enforcing the system vis-a-vis the millions of suppliers worldwide.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: By designing the system as we have, I think it does facilitate enforcement and implementation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon and Mr Melvin Yong also asked how we will enforce compliance for overseas vendors for B2C services.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: IRAS will make use of various information sources to identify and engage potential registrants as well as to verify the GST reporting by these businesses.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Similar to domestic traders, business audits will be conducted by IRAS on a risk-based approach.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We already do this for our regular GST regime.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will extend this for OVR as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: IRAS can also use provisions in bilateral tax agreements to obtain information on overseas vendors from other tax jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In the event of non-compliance, the existing penalty and enforcement regime under the GST Act will apply.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: IRAS will raise additional tax assessments, apply penalties and recover the outstanding tax payable directly or through the appointment of agents.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are not the first country to do this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we have learnt from the experiences of many other jurisdictions, including Australia, New Zealand and South Korea, which apply similar penalty regimes to non-resident registrants, as with domestic businesses.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That said, as I highlighted earlier, many of these overseas businesses have experience meeting similar VAT/GST obligations in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Many of them are familiar because we are not the first country and they have experience meeting similar GST obligations in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we do not anticipate significant compliance issues.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Experience from other jurisdictions show that these multinational businesses are likely to comply to avoid reputational damage.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On Dr Intan Mokhtar's queries, not all digital services consumed in Singapore, be it B2B or B2C, are supplied by GST registered businesses.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, there are non-GST registered suppliers for such services.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We do not track the number of these services.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They may be small companies or even individual entrepreneurs providing such services on various online platforms.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, Dr Intan Mokhtar asked about such non-GST registered businesses and the concern whether they may charge GST on their sales.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why we currently impose penalties and fines on all unauthorised GST collection offences under the GST Act.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This applies for both local and overseas suppliers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This applies even in the existing GST regime.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is the responsibility of GST-registered businesses to apply the correct GST treatment on their transactions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That way, we make the GST system a resilient one in generating tax revenue to fund public services.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I should also explain that it is not just about the delta in revenue collection because this move also seeks to defend our current revenue base from being eroded as more and more transactions move online.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, if we were not to do anything, potentially, the revenue base may get more and more eroded and we may be losing more revenue.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we have to make this move now to defend our current revenue base from being eroded.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon made the comment that overseas businesses may decide to stop their sales to Singapore as a result of the tax measure.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It may be a concern for some, but I should highlight as I said earlier that, firstly, we are not the first country to impose GST on imported services.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Other jurisdictions have done so, and this is in line with the global movement towards taxation of the digital economy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Tax is important but there are many other fundamental attributes, such as our high digital penetration, our sophisticated and tech-savvy consumers, our extensive connectivity as well as our robust IT and logistics infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, overall, we are still in a very strong position to be a regional e-commerce hub.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Melvin Yong raised queries relating to the taxation of online advertising services and also asked whether consultancy and advisory services will be subject to GST under the new regime.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Briefly, the scope of tax under OVR is consistent with current GST rules and how they are applied to local suppliers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, for online advertising services, whether or not GST is applicable depends on the place of circulation of the advertisement.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Under existing rules, media advertisement that is circulated substantially or wholly outside Singapore qualify for zero-rating.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Likewise, if provided by overseas suppliers, such advertising services are not subject to GST.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we are using the current GST rules and if it is zero-rated locally, then when supplied under OVR, it will not be subject to GST.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: By the same logic, for advertisements placed on the Internet, we regard the viewer access is generally global.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Such advertisements can qualify for zero-rating and, correspondingly, will not be subject to GST under the OVR regime.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Melvin Yong asked whether there are plans to extend the GST measures to low-value imported goods.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Most jurisdictions have in place an import relief threshold for imports of goods via air and post.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Imported goods below this threshold will not be subject to GST, so as to facilitate clearance at the border, and to ease administrative costs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Below $400, there is no need for GST.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The taxation of low-value goods is a relatively new tax development and we are monitoring international developments on this front.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Switzerland and New Zealand, and the EU have indicated plans to do so in 2019 and 2021 respectively.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, again, as we have done for imported services, we first look at what other jurisdictions have done, we study their experiences and then, we learn from these experiences to see what can be done in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is what we are doing with regard to the GST measure for low-value imported goods.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon shared his concern on a "digital divide".

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is, indeed, something that all of us ought to be concerned about.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are several ways we are dealing with this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, we have in place the permanent GST Voucher (GSTV) scheme that provides annual assistance to citizens.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This offsets GST expenses for many Singaporeans, especially retiree and lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We review the GSTV scheme regularly to ensure that there is adequate assistance for the lower income.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, as Singapore becomes more connected, the Government will also do more to ensure digital inclusion and accessibility.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are already many programmes under the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) which provide lower-income households with subsidised broadband and devices and access to the Internet.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In addition, the Silver Infocomm Initiative offers affordable IT classes to equip seniors with relevant basic digital skills.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And, of course, Singaporeans can use their SkillsFuture Credit to offset course fees, including digital courses offered by online platforms.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have debated this in the House every time we have a Budget and when we talk about the GST regime.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Basically, we agree fully with the objective of having an overall tax and transfer system that is progressive, one where we give more help to those who have less.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think all of us share fully that intent.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we have also seen the experience of other countries with a multi-tiered GST system which introduces immense complexities in trying to define what are regarded as basic essentials and what are to be treated as luxury goods.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Besides luxury items, Dr Intan Mokhtar also proposed higher consumption tax rates for alcoholic beverages and tobacco products.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are mindful of the negative externalities arising from the consumption of such products, as the Member has highlighted and, in fact, these are already taken into account by way of excise duties.
